title: About Me
text: I’m a data analyst based in Miami, working in the cruise industry. At Royal Caribbean Group I work on fleet deployment and itinerary planning, where a single schedule change can affect ports, fuel, crew and guests at the same time. Most of my day is spent pulling that information together in SQL, Python, Excel and Power BI so the team can see the trade-offs clearly before making a call.

How I got here
I started with a bachelor’s degree in finance from Florida International University, which gave me a solid base in financial modeling and economics. Before the cruise industry, I worked at Parkland, where I built KPI reports, ran root cause analysis on operational problems and helped develop pricing strategies. I then moved to Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings, working on deployment and revenue analysis and building Tableau dashboards that revenue and strategy teams used every week. That work led me to my current role at Royal Caribbean Group.

title: About Me
text:
What I’m working toward
My goal is to move into data science and machine learning roles. Much of the analysis I do today explains what happened and why. I want to get better at the predictive side: building models that forecast demand, flag risks early and help teams plan ahead instead of reacting. The master’s program at Boston University has given me hands-on practice with classification models, Apache Spark, cloud computing on AWS and generative AI, and I apply those skills to real problems whenever I can.

title: Weekly Planning File Consolidation
text:
The problem
Planning data lives in separate tabs for each ship, and combining it into one view is a recurring weekly task. Port names are also spelled differently from one source to another, which makes comparisons error-prone.

title: Weekly Planning File Consolidation
text:
What I did

Wrote a Python script that reads every ship’s tab, standardizes the columns and stacks them into one combined dataset.
Added fuzzy matching to line up port names that are spelled differently, so the combined file can be checked against the itinerary system of record.
Built it to run the same way every week, so the output is consistent and easy to repeat.

title: Weekly Planning File Consolidation
text:
Results
The script cut analysis time by 30% and gives the team one consistent dataset to work from every week.

title: Weekly Planning File Consolidation
text:
What I learned
Real-world text is messy. A good automation script has to expect variations, like abbreviations and spelling differences, instead of assuming every source follows the same format.

title: Career Evaluation Website
text:
The problem
Job seekers in analytics see thousands of postings but very little structure: which roles pay more, which skills matter and where the jobs actually are. Our team set out to build a site that answers those questions for one industry, Computer Systems Design and Related Services (NAICS 5415).

title: Career Evaluation Website
text:
What I did

Built the data pipeline that filters a 504,208-row job postings extract down to a clean, 12-month panel of 1,790 postings for NAICS 5415.
Wrote the location and salary cleaning scripts, including a fix for Washington, DC postings that were being counted as Washington State.
Added role family and years of experience fields so the team could compare roles side by side.
Proposed switching industries after finding that our first choice, pharmaceutical manufacturing, had only 39 postings in the data.
Wrote the literature review that frames why the project matters.

title: Career Evaluation Website
text:
Results
The pipeline gives the team one consistent dataset that every page of the site draws from, and the numbers in the text are computed from the data instead of typed in by hand.

title: Career Evaluation Website
text:
What I learned
Most of the work in a data product happens before the first chart. Small cleaning decisions, like how to read a location field, can quietly change every number downstream, so I now check edge cases early and write down every rule I apply.

title: Job Market Analytics with Apache Spark
text:
The problem
Practice building analytics end to end in the cloud on a job postings dataset that is too large for a spreadsheet, and turn it into clear answers about pay and demand.

title: Job Market Analytics with Apache Spark
text:
What I did

Set up an AWS EC2 instance with PySpark, a Python virtual environment and a Git workflow, and worked on it remotely from VS Code.
Modeled the postings as a star schema in Spark SQL and wrote four queries on salary and demand across industries and states.
Converted hourly, weekly and monthly pay to annual salaries and bounded outliers at the 99.5th percentile.
Cleaned state names with a lookup table that fixed abbreviations and split city names.
In a second analysis, recovered years of experience from job description text with regular expressions when the structured fields were empty, then charted salary by industry, education, experience and remote status.
Added swap space after Spark ran out of memory on the full dataset.

title: Job Market Analytics with Apache Spark
text:
Results
Reproducible reports rendered to HTML, Word and PDF from one Quarto source, with interactive charts on the web and static images in the documents.

title: Job Market Analytics with Apache Spark
text:
What I learned
Working at scale changes your habits. I now check data quality before modeling, keep the raw data untouched and expect infrastructure issues, like memory and sessions, to be part of the job rather than a surprise.
The code stays private under the course’s academic integrity policy.

title: Competitor Deployment Explorer
text:
The problem
Our deployment team needed to understand how competitors use key regions, but the source data was a flat table of 101,067 port-call rows across 9,068 voyages. It had no coordinates or distances, port names were inconsistent and some ports were miscoded. Answering questions like “what is each line’s most common turnaround pair in the Adriatic?” or “is this Panama Canal sailing a product or a repositioning?” meant manual spreadsheet work.

title: Competitor Deployment Explorer
text:
What it does
I built a tool with three views, all driven by one shared set of filters: year, region, competitor, ship, itinerary, cruise ID, embark and debark port, open or closed jaw, port, country, nights and date range.

Sailing Routes plots any sailing on a map. Routes follow the sea around land and through canals and straits, and they respect real limits: ships too wide for the Corinth Canal go around the Peloponnese instead. A day-by-day panel shows ship size and estimated distances, and a “previous and next” overlay shows how each ship moves between deployments.
Pivot works like an Excel pivot table in the browser. Any field can be a row or a column, measuring sailings, capacity (APCD), nights or distance as sums, averages or percentages, with CSV export.
Dashboard shows six headline figures and eight interactive charts, such as capacity by competitor and seasonality by month. Clicking any bar or pivot cell filters the whole page.

title: Competitor Deployment Explorer
text:
How I built it

Data pipeline (Python and pandas): I rebuilt each sailing’s stops from the raw port-call records and geocoded about 900 ports using our port table, the UN’s register of port locations (UN/LOCODE) and GeoNames. When several places shared a name, I picked the one closest to the neighboring calls.
Data quality: I added a plausibility check based on the speed a ship would need between two calls. It caught miscoded ports such as Trogir entered for Trondheim, Dublin for Dubrovnik, and Cartagena, Spain confused with Cartagena, Colombia. I log every correction.
Front end: a single self-contained web page built with D3.js and TopoJSON, with a custom route-finding algorithm that steers around land. It works on desktop and mobile.
Business rules: I defined the rules our team cares about: each line’s most common turnaround pair, standalone versus repositioning sailings based on each ship’s surrounding voyages, full versus half Panama Canal transits, Venice mid-cruise calls and a set of direct competitors.
Validation: I cross-check every filter value and count against the companion Excel workbook, sailing by sailing. Pivot totals tie to the workbook, distances come from one shared calculation, and browser tests run automatically with Playwright.

title: Competitor Deployment Explorer
text:
Results

Questions about regions and competitors that used to take manual spreadsheet work now take a few clicks.
I also delivered an Excel workbook with sailing-level data, day-by-day itineraries, ship specs, top turnaround pairs and the correction log, plus executive slides profiling each region by competitor: round trip versus open jaw, standalone versus repositioning, average length, ship size and most common turnaround pair.

title: Competitor Deployment Explorer
text:
What I learned
I owned the business questions, data rules and success criteria, and I reviewed every output against what I know from operations. That review caught issues like unrealistic canal routings and misclassified sailings. I used Claude as a coding assistant to speed up the build. My biggest takeaway: AI makes building faster, but domain knowledge is what makes the results trustworthy.

title: Zurich Airbnb Classification
text:
The problem
Can listing data predict things guests care about? We asked two questions: does a listing offer a dedicated workspace, and how quickly does the host respond to messages?

title: Zurich Airbnb Classification
text:
What I did
k-nearest neighbors (workspace or not). Used 10 numeric predictors and a stratified 70/30 split, scaled the features on the training data only to avoid leakage, and tested odd values of k from 1 to 51 with 10-fold cross-validation. The best was k = 5.
Decision tree (host response time, four classes). Used 16 predictors and tuned cost-complexity pruning with 10-fold cross-validation, which produced a tree 7 levels deep with 19 leaves.

title: Zurich Airbnb Classification
text:
Results



Model
Test accuracy
Naive baseline
Lift




KNN, dedicated workspace
60.8%
58.7%
+2.1 points


Decision tree, response time
73.9%
61.9%
+12.0 points



The tree clearly beat its baseline, with host behavior variables driving most of its splits. The KNN model only edged past its baseline, which is a finding in itself: listing numbers say little about which amenities a place offers.

title: Zurich Airbnb Classification
text:
What I learned
Always report the baseline. A model with 60% accuracy sounds fine until you see that guessing the most common answer gets you 59%. Comparing against a naive benchmark keeps the results honest.
